claim: NbAGO4-1 and NbAGO4-2 were identified as associated to V2-GFP by affinity purification followed by mass spectrometry (AP-MS).
source: Interestingly, we identified the two AGO4 paralogs in N. benthamiana (NbAGO4-1 and NbAGO4-2) as associated to V2-GFP (Figure 1A; Wang et al., 2017a)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AP-MS experiments shown in Figure 1A and cited from Wang et al., 2017a.

claim: V2-GFP interacts with 3xHA-NbAGO4-1 and 3xHA-NbAGO4-2 in co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: 3xHA-NbAGO4-1 and 3xHA-NbAGO4-2 specifically interact with V2-GFP in co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays upon transient expression in N. benthamiana.

claim: NbAGO4-1 and NbAGO4-2 interact with V2 in split-luciferase assays.
source: NbAGO4-1 and NbAGO4-2 interact with V2 in split-luciferase assays.

claim: There are four AGO4 orthologues in tomato (SlAGO4a-d).

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bai et al., 2012 and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: All four SlAGO4-encoding genes are expressed in basal conditions in tomato leaves.
source: All four SlAGO4-encoding genes are expressed in basal conditions in tomato leaves, although SlAGO4c and d show low expression levels
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SlAGO4c and d show low expression levels in basal conditions in tomato leaves.
source: All four SlAGO4-encoding genes are expressed in basal conditions in tomato leaves, although SlAGO4c and d show low expression levels
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SlAGO4b, c, and d are slightly upregulated by TYLCV infection.
source: SlAGO4b, c, and d are slightly upregulated by TYLCV infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SlAGO4a, SlAGO4b, and SlAGO4d interact with V2 in co-IP assays.

evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SlAGO4a and SlAGO4b interact with V2 in split-luciferase assays.
source: SlAGO4a, SlAGO4b, and SlAGO4d were cloned and the encoded proteins confirmed as interactors of V2 in co-IP and split-luciferase assays (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by split-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: V2 interacts with AGO4 in two host species, tomato and N. benthamiana.
source: Our results therefore show that V2 interacts with AGO4 in two host species, tomato and N. benthamiana.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-IP and split-luciferase assays shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: V2 is required for full infectivity in both tomato and N. benthamiana.
source: In agreement with previous results (Wartig et al., 1997), V2 is required for full infectivity in both tomato and N. benthamiana, since the V2 null mutant accumulates to very low levels and produces no noticeable symptoms in systemic infections (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and cited from Wartig et al., 1997.

claim: The V2 null mutant accumulates to very low levels in systemic infections.
source: In agreement with previous results (Wartig et al., 1997), V2 is required for full infectivity in both tomato and N. benthamiana, since the V2 null mutant accumulates to very low levels and produces no noticeable symptoms in systemic infections (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The V2 null mutant produces no noticeable symptoms in systemic infections.
source: In agreement with previous results (Wartig et al., 1997), V2 is required for full infectivity in both tomato and N. benthamiana, since the V2 null mutant accumulates to very low levels and produces no noticeable symptoms in systemic infections (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: VIGS efficiently knocked-down both NbAGO4 orthologues.
source: VIGS efficiently knocked-down both NbAGO4 orthologues, but did not affect accumulation of the transcript of the close homologue NbAGO6 (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VIGS of NbAGO4 did not affect accumulation of the transcript of the close homologue NbAGO6.
source: VIGS efficiently knocked-down both NbAGO4 orthologues, but did not affect accumulation of the transcript of the close homologue NbAGO6 (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AGO4-silenced plants did not display any obvious developmental abnormalities.
source: AGO4-silenced plants did not display any obvious developmental abnormalities (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of NbAGO4-1 or NbAGO4-2 was not affected by TYLCV infection.
source: Expression of NbAGO4-1 or NbAGO4-2 was not affected by TYLCV infection, neither in silenced nor in non-silenced plants (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Mutation in V2 does not affect viral replication.
source: Mutation in V2 does not affect viral replication (Wartig et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wartig et al., 1997.

claim: Viral accumulation in local infections in N. benthamiana was not different between the wild-type virus and the V2 null mutant virus.
source: Mutation in V2 does not affect viral replication (Wartig et al., 1997), and therefore viral accumulation in local infections in N. benthamiana (leaf patch agroinfiltration assays; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1) was not different between the wild-type virus and the V2 null mutant virus (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AGO4 silencing led to a not statistically significant but reproducible trend to higher viral accumulation in local infections.
source: in both cases, AGO4 silencing led to a not statistically significant but reproducible trend to higher viral accumulation, suggesting an antiviral role for AGO4 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AGO4 has an antiviral role.
source: in both cases, AGO4 silencing led to a not statistically significant but reproducible trend to higher viral accumulation, suggesting an antiviral role for AGO4 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing increases viral accumulation.

claim: AGO4 silencing mildly increased viral accumulation of the wild-type TYLCV (1.33-fold) in systemic infections.
source: Interestingly, in systemic infections (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), AGO4 silencing mildly increased viral accumulation of the wild-type TYLCV (1.33-fold), but dramatically improved performance of the V2 null mutant virus (3.23-fold), suggesting that one of the main roles of V2 during the viral infection is the suppression of AGO4 function (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: AGO4 silencing dramatically improved performance of the V2 null mutant virus (3.23-fold) in systemic infections.
source: Interestingly, in systemic infections (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), AGO4 silencing mildly increased viral accumulation of the wild-type TYLCV (1.33-fold), but dramatically improved performance of the V2 null mutant virus (3.23-fold), suggesting that one of the main roles of V2 during the viral infection is the suppression of AGO4 function (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: One of the main roles of V2 during the viral infection is the suppression of AGO4 function.
source: Interestingly, in systemic infections (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), AGO4 silencing mildly increased viral accumulation of the wild-type TYLCV (1.33-fold), but dramatically improved performance of the V2 null mutant virus (3.23-fold), suggesting that one of the main roles of V2 during the viral infection is the suppression of AGO4 function (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing dramatically complements the V2 null mutant.

claim: Cytosine methylation in the intergenic region of the wild-type viral genome in all contexts (CG, CHG, and CHH) was almost undetectable in local infections at 3 or 9 days post-inoculation.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, cytosine methylation in this region in all contexts (CG, CHG, and CHH) was almost undetectable in the wild-type viral genome in local infections at 3 or 9 days post-inoculation (dpi)
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cytosine methylation in the intergenic region of the V2 null mutant viral genome reached ~60% at 3 dpi and ~80% at 9 dpi in local infections.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, cytosine methylation in this region in all contexts (CG, CHG, and CHH) was almost undetectable in the wild-type viral genome in local infections at 3 or 9 days post-inoculation (dpi), while it reached ~60% and~80%, respectively, in the V2 null mutant (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: V2 can prevent or revert methylation of the viral genome during the infection.
source: These results indicate that V2 can prevent or revert methylation of the viral genome during the infection, which occurs rapidly in the absence of this protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that methylation is high in the V2 null mutant but low in wild-type virus.

claim: Methylation of the viral genome occurs rapidly in the absence of V2.
source: These results indicate that V2 can prevent or revert methylation of the viral genome during the infection, which occurs rapidly in the absence of this protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing high methylation at 3 dpi in the V2 null mutant.

claim: AGO4 silencing resulted in a ~30% decrease in the percentage of methylated cytosines in all contexts in the V2 null mutant in local infections.
source: Strikingly, AGO4 silencing resulted in a ~30% decrease in the percentage of methylated cytosines in all contexts (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knock-down of AGO4 can partially complement the lack of V2 at the level of the viral methylation state.
source: indicating that knock-down of AGO4 can partially complement the lack of V2 at the level of the viral methylation state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing reduces methylation in the V2 null mutant.

claim: Methylation of the viral DNA at least partially depends on AGO4 function.
source: This complementation suggests that (a) methylation of the viral DNA at least partially depends on AGO4 function and (b) V2 can at least partially counter AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral DNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing reduces viral DNA methylation.

claim: V2 can at least partially counter AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral DNA.
source: This complementation suggests that (a) methylation of the viral DNA at least partially depends on AGO4 function and (b) V2 can at least partially counter AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral DNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing partially complements the V2 null mutant.

claim: In systemic infections in N. benthamiana, methylation of the wild-type viral genome could be detected at ~8–23% in all contexts.
source: As opposed to short-timed local infections, in systemic infections in N. benthamiana, which require longer timespans and involve viral cell-to-cell and long-distance movement, methylation of the wild-type viral genome could be detected at ~8–23% in all contexts (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The methylation level of the wild-type viral genome tends to decrease upon AGO4 silencing in systemic infections.
source: Interestingly, the methylation level tends to decrease upon AGO4 silencing; this reduction (~12–31%) brings the methylation of the V2 null mutant genome back to wild type-like levels, again supporting the idea that AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral genome occurs during the infection and is partially countered by V2.
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AGO4 silencing brings the methylation of the V2 null mutant genome back to wild type-like levels in systemic infections.
source: Interestingly, the methylation level tends to decrease upon AGO4 silencing; this reduction (~12–31%) brings the methylation of the V2 null mutant genome back to wild type-like levels, again supporting the idea that AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral genome occurs during the infection and is partially countered by V2.
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral genome occurs during the infection and is partially countered by V2.
source: Interestingly, the methylation level tends to decrease upon AGO4 silencing; this reduction (~12–31%) brings the methylation of the V2 null mutant genome back to wild type-like levels, again supporting the idea that AGO4-dependent methylation of the viral genome occurs during the infection and is partially countered by V2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGO4 silencing reduces methylation in both wild-type and V2 null mutant infections.

claim: The detected decrease in methylation correlates with the enhanced viral accumulation in the AGO4-silenced plants.
source: Notably, the detected decrease in methylation correlates with the enhanced viral accumulation in the AGO4-silenced plants (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between methylation data (Figure 4C) and viral accumulation data (Figure 3F).

claim: 3xFLAG-NbAGO4-1 can bind both the IR and the V2-encoding region of the viral genome in the absence of V2.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, 3xFLAG-NbAGO4-1 could bind both the IR and the V2-encoding region of the viral genome in the absence of V2 (TYLCV-V2null), but the signal decreased to background levels when V2 was present (TYLCV).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AGO4 binding to the viral genome is impaired by the virus-encoded V2 protein.
source: Therefore, AGO4 has the capacity to bind the viral DNA molecule, but this binding is impaired by the virus-encoded V2 protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AGO4 binding in the TYLCV V2 null mutant correlates with the detected increase in viral DNA methylation.
source: AGO4 binding in the TYLCV V2 null mutant hence correlates with the detected increase in viral DNA methylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between ChIP data (Figure 5A) and methylation data (Figure 4A).

claim: The presence of V2 in the wild-type virus causes a decrease in the binding of AGO4 to RNA molecules derived from the non-coding intergenic region (IR) and the adjacent V2 ORF.
source: For this purpose, we performed RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) using 3xFLAG-NbAGO4-1 in locally infected samples; our results indicate that the presence of V2 in the wild-type virus causes a decrease in the binding of AGO4 to RNA molecules derived from the non-coding intergenic region (IR) and the adjacent V2 ORF (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Infected samples contained both 21- and 24-nt vsiRNA.
source: While infected samples contained both 21- and 24-nt vsiRNA, and the occurrence and accumulation of these sRNA species was not affected by the presence of virus-encoded V2, mostly 24-nt vsiRNA co-immunoprecipitated with AGO4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The occurrence and accumulation of vsiRNA species was not affected by the presence of virus-encoded V2.
source: While infected samples contained both 21- and 24-nt vsiRNA, and the occurrence and accumulation of these sRNA species was not affected by the presence of virus-encoded V2, mostly 24-nt vsiRNA co-immunoprecipitated with AGO4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mostly 24-nt vsiRNA co-immunoprecipitated with AGO4.
source: While infected samples contained both 21- and 24-nt vsiRNA, and the occurrence and accumulation of these sRNA species was not affected by the presence of virus-encoded V2, mostly 24-nt vsiRNA co-immunoprecipitated with AGO4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A higher amount of vsiRNA associated to AGO4 in the samples infected with the wild-type virus.
source: Interestingly, a higher amount of vsiRNA associated to AGO4 in the samples infected with the wild-type virus (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: V2 does not affect the production or accumulation of vsiRNA.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that V2 does not affect the production or accumulation of vsiRNA, nor does it hamper loading of the vsiRNA molecules into AGO4, but it interferes with binding of this protein to the viral RNA and genome in order to suppress DNA methylation and promote virulence.
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: V2 does not hamper loading of the vsiRNA molecules into AGO4.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that V2 does not affect the production or accumulation of vsiRNA, nor does it hamper loading of the vsiRNA molecules into AGO4, but it interferes with binding of this protein to the viral RNA and genome in order to suppress DNA methylation and promote virulence.
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: V2 interferes with binding of AGO4 to the viral RNA and genome in order to suppress DNA methylation and promote virulence.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that V2 does not affect the production or accumulation of vsiRNA, nor does it hamper loading of the vsiRNA molecules into AGO4, but it interferes with binding of this protein to the viral RNA and genome in order to suppress DNA methylation and promote virulence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of ChIP, RIP, and northern blot experiments.

claim: AGO4 has been shown to co-localize with its interactor NRPE1 (NRPD1b), a subunit of Pol V, in the Cajal body in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, AGO4 has been shown to co-localize with its interactor NRPE1 (NRPD1b), a subunit of Pol V, in the Cajal body, which was then suggested to be a center for the assembly of AGO4/NRPE1/siRNA complexes, enabling RdDM at target loci (Li et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008 and Li et al., 2006.

claim: The Cajal body was suggested to be a center for the assembly of AGO4/NRPE1/siRNA complexes, enabling RdDM at target loci.
source: In Arabidopsis, AGO4 has been shown to co-localize with its interactor NRPE1 (NRPD1b), a subunit of Pol V, in the Cajal body, which was then suggested to be a center for the assembly of AGO4/NRPE1/siRNA complexes, enabling RdDM at target loci (Li et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008 and Li et al., 2006.

claim: Both V2-GFP and the different RFP-AGO4 orthologues from N. benthamiana and tomato co-localize in a distinct subnuclear compartment, identified as the Cajal body.
source: Interestingly, both V2-GFP and the different RFP-AGO4 orthologues from N. benthamiana and tomato co-localize in a distinct subnuclear compartment, identified as the Cajal body by the accumulation of the nucleolus and Cajal body marker fibrillarin (Barneche et al., 2000), upon transient expression in N. benthamiana (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and citation to Barneche et al., 2000.

claim: Most of nuclear V2-GFP accumulates in the Cajal body, although some fluorescence can be detected in the nucleoplasm.
source: Of note, most of nuclear V2-GFP accumulates in the Cajal body, although some fluorescence can be detected in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All AGO4 orthologues are distributed throughout the nucleoplasm and absent from the nucleolus.
source: All AGO4 orthologues are distributed throughout the nucleoplasm and absent from the nucleolus; clear Cajal body localization can be detected for NbAGO4-1, NbAGO4-2, SlAGO4a, and SlAGO4b, while Cajal body localization of SlAGO4d is less conspicuous (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Clear Cajal body localization can be detected for NbAGO4-1, NbAGO4-2, SlAGO4a, and SlAGO4b.
source: All AGO4 orthologues are distributed throughout the nucleoplasm and absent from the nucleolus; clear Cajal body localization can be detected for NbAGO4-1, NbAGO4-2, SlAGO4a, and SlAGO4b, while Cajal body localization of SlAGO4d is less conspicuous (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cajal body localization of SlAGO4d is less conspicuous.
source: All AGO4 orthologues are distributed throughout the nucleoplasm and absent from the nucleolus; clear Cajal body localization can be detected for NbAGO4-1, NbAGO4-2, SlAGO4a, and SlAGO4b, while Cajal body localization of SlAGO4d is less conspicuous (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The association between V2 and AGO4 occurs mostly or exclusively in the Cajal body.
source: Analysis of the V2/AGO4 interaction by bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), which is based on visualization and hence provides spatial information, unveiled that, strikingly, the association between these two proteins occurs mostly or exclusively in the Cajal body, where V2 homotypic interactions also occur (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: V2 homotypic interactions occur in the Cajal body.
source: Analysis of the V2/AGO4 interaction by bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), which is based on visualization and hence provides spatial information, unveiled that, strikingly, the association between these two proteins occurs mostly or exclusively in the Cajal body, where V2 homotypic interactions also occur (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GFP-V2 does not localize to the Cajal body.
source: In order to evaluate the relevance of the Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction, we took advantage of the fact that a GFP-V2 fusion protein, as opposed to the previously mentioned V2-GFP, does not localize to the Cajal body (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—videos 1 and 2), otherwise showing an indistinguishable subcellular distribution pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: GFP-V2 shows an indistinguishable subcellular distribution pattern compared to V2-GFP, except for Cajal body localization.
source: In order to evaluate the relevance of the Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction, we took advantage of the fact that a GFP-V2 fusion protein, as opposed to the previously mentioned V2-GFP, does not localize to the Cajal body (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—videos 1 and 2), otherwise showing an indistinguishable subcellular distribution pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: GFP-V2 still interacts with AGO4 in co-IP assays.
source: Importantly, GFP-V2 still interacts with AGO4 in co-IP assays (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only the Cajal body-localized V2-GFP, but not GFP-V2, can complement a null mutation in V2 in terms of suppression of methylation of the viral genome.
source: Nevertheless, only the Cajal body-localized V2-GFP, but not GFP-V2, can complement a null mutation in V2 in terms of suppression of methylation of the viral genome (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C)
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction is essential for V2 to exert its function.
source: indicating that the Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction is essential for V2 to exert its function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only Cajal body-localized V2-GFP can suppress viral DNA methylation.

claim: Silencing of coilin resulted in the apparent disappearance of Cajal bodies.
source: As expected, silencing coilin (Figure 7D) resulted in the apparent disappearance of Cajal bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Methylation of the IR of the viral genome in the V2 mutant virus was largely decreased by silencing of coilin.
source: Strikingly, however, methylation of the IR of the viral genome in the V2 mutant virus was largely decreased by silencing of coilin (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Efficient methylation of the viral genome requires intact Cajal bodies.
source: suggesting that efficient methylation of the viral genome requires intact Cajal bodies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that coilin silencing reduces viral DNA methylation.

claim: HDA6 does not localize to the Cajal body.
source: Notably, the described V2 interactor HDA6 does not localize to the Cajal body (Figure 7—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The V2-HDA6 complexes seem to localize outside of the nucleus.
source: and the V2-HDA6 complexes seem to localize outside of the nucleus (Wang et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: The detected Cajal body-dependent effects rely on AGO4 and not HDA6.
source: Notably, the described V2 interactor HDA6 does not localize to the Cajal body (Figure 7—figure supplement 3) and the V2-HDA6 complexes seem to localize outside of the nucleus (Wang et al., 2018), supporting the idea that the detected Cajal body-dependent effects rely on AGO4 and not HDA6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HDA6 does not localize to the Cajal body.

claim: Establishment of de novo DNA methylation is regulated by the RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) pathway in plants.
source: In plants, establishment of de novo DNA methylation is believed to be regulated by the RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about plant DNA methylation.

claim: RdDM machinery is known to concentrate in the Cajal body.
source: RdDM machinery is known to concentrate in the Cajal body, but the biological significance of this localization has remained elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Methylation of the TYLCV genome requires the Cajal body in Nicotiana benthamiana cells.
source: Here, we show that the antiviral methylation of the Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) genome requires the Cajal body in Nicotiana benthamiana cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that coilin silencing reduces viral DNA methylation.

claim: V2 interacts with the central RdDM component AGO4.
source: Methylation of the viral genome is countered by a virus-encoded protein, V2, which interacts with the central RdDM component AGO4
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP, split-luciferase, and BiFC data.

claim: V2 interferes with AGO4 binding to the viral DNA.
source: Methylation of the viral genome is countered by a virus-encoded protein, V2, which interacts with the central RdDM component AGO4, interfering with its binding to the viral DNA
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction is necessary for the viral protein to exert this function.
source: Cajal body localization of the V2-AGO4 interaction is necessary for the viral protein to exert this function.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that only Cajal body-localized V2-GFP can suppress viral DNA methylation.

claim: The canonical RdDM pathway requires the activity of two plant-specific RNA polymerase II-related enzymes, Pol IV and Pol V.
source: The canonical RdDM pathway requires the activity of two plant-specific RNA polymerase II-related enzymes, Pol IV and Pol V, and leads to cytosine methylation in a sequence-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the RdDM pathway.

claim: Pol IV generates RNA transcripts subsequently converted to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) by RDR2.
source: Pol IV generates RNA transcripts subsequently converted to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) by RDR2 (Haag et al., 2012; Law et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haag et al., 2012 and Law et al., 2011.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Böhmdorfer et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2005; Gao et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: AGO4 recruits the de novo methyltransferase DRM2.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Böhmdorfer et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2005; Gao et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: DRM2 catalyses methylation of adjacent DNA sequences.
source: which in turn catalyses methylation of adjacent DNA sequences.
